entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Homeric Hymns are a collection of ancient Greek poems attributed to Homer, composed between c. 800 BCE and c. 500 CE.

These sacred songs were recited during religious rituals and festivals in ancient Greece, with the most famous being the Iliad and the Odyssey.

The hymns contain a wealth of information about the mythology and culture of the time, providing insights into the human condition, nature, and the gods.

This poetic legacy has had a profound impact on Western literature and continues to influence art, music, and poetry to this day.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Homeric Hymns are a collection of 33 ancient Greek hymns in dactylic hexameter attributed in antiquity to Homer — though modern scholarship recognises them as the work of various anonymous poets composed over a wide span of time (7th–5th centuries BCE, with some possibly earlier and the Hymn to Hermes perhaps as late as the 6th century BCE). The Hymns are addressed to the major Greek deities — the great hymns to Demeter, Apollo, Hermes, and Aphrodite are the longest and most significant, while the shorter hymns to Dionysus, Ares, Athena, Poseidon, and others vary in length from a few lines to several hundred. The Hymns served as preludes (prooimia) to epic recitation — bards would perform a hymn to the appropriate deity before reciting an epic narrative, inviting divine favour — and they preserve some of the earliest surviving extended narratives of Greek mythology.

The Homeric Hymn to Demeter (7th century BCE, approximately 495 lines) is the primary literary source for the myth of Persephone's abduction by Hades and Demeter's search for her daughter — the aetiological myth of the Eleusinian Mysteries (the most important mystery cult of ancient Greece) and the Greek explanation of the seasons (Persephone's annual return from the underworld brings spring; her annual descent brings winter). The Hymn to Demeter's detailed description of the Eleusinian rites — the wandering of Demeter, her reception at Eleusis, the institution of the Mysteries — makes it the most important literary source for our knowledge of the Eleusinian cult.

The Homeric Hymn to Apollo (two sections traditionally distinguished as the 'Delian' and 'Pythian' hymns) narrates the birth of Apollo on Delos and his establishment of the Delphic Oracle — making it the primary literary source for the foundation mythology of the two most important Apolline sanctuaries in the Greek world.
